mcqs.question: Why does IEEE-754 store the exponent as a biased value instead of two's complement?
options: Biasing makes the exponent field shorter
It lets hardware compare two same-sign floats correctly using ordinary unsigned integer comparison on the raw bits
Two's complement cannot represent negative exponents
It was required to keep backward compatibility with 16-bit floats
mcqs.explanation: A biased exponent preserves numeric ordering under plain unsigned bit-pattern comparison, so no special float-comparison circuitry is needed. Two's complement absolutely can represent negative numbers — that's not the limitation; the issue is it would break bitwise-comparison ordering.

mcqs.question: A 32-bit float has exponent bits 10000010 (binary). What is the actual (unbiased) exponent?
mcqs.explanation: 10000010 in binary is 130; subtracting the single-precision bias of 127 gives an actual exponent of 3.

mcqs.question: What distinguishes a denormal (subnormal) float from a normal one?
options: Denormals use a different sign convention
Denormals have exponent bits all zero and no implicit leading 1, letting them represent values closer to zero than any normal number
Denormals are simply floats with a negative value
Denormals use twice as many mantissa bits as normal floats
mcqs.explanation: Denormals drop the usual implicit-1 assumption, trading some precision to represent a graduated range of values between zero and the smallest normal float, instead of underflowing straight to zero.

mcqs.question: What does `x == x` evaluate to when x is NaN in IEEE-754?
options: Always true, since equality is reflexive
False — by definition, NaN never compares equal to anything, including itself
It's undefined behavior in every language
mcqs.explanation: IEEE-754 defines NaN comparisons (other than != ) to always be false, including self-comparison — this is intentional, so that `x != x` becomes a valid (if surprising) way to test for NaN.
